name: Extraction-free orthodontics

card.summary: Straightening teeth by expanding or distalizing the arches instead of removing premolars, which people use to keep the lips, midface and profile looking full and forward.
card.note: Whether extractions are needed depends on crowding, protrusion and jaw relationships; an orthodontist's diagnosis decides.

quick.overview:
Extraction-free (non-extraction) orthodontics is a treatment plan in which crowded or misaligned teeth are aligned without pulling teeth, usually premolars. Space is made by widening the dental arches, tilting teeth forward, moving molars backward or slightly reducing tooth width instead.

In looksmaxxing circles it is valued as a way to preserve forward facial support: lips, cheeks and the profile. Studies of non-extraction treatment report that lips tend to move forward and down in adolescents, while adults show smaller changes. Some patients with strongly protruding teeth are treated with extractions to pull the front teeth back, so the choice is made case by case.
quick.how: Patients are assessed with photographs, X-rays and cephalometric measurements. A non-extraction plan can use braces or clear aligners with arch expansion, interproximal reduction, molar distalization (often with temporary anchorage screws) or palatal expanders in growing patients. Treatment commonly runs from about one to two years depending on the case.
quick.risks: Non-extraction plans can leave teeth more proclined, and one 2025 study examined open gingival embrasures (small gaps at the gum line) after non-extraction treatment. Relapse and gum recession are discussed in orthodontic literature. Extraction is sometimes the recommended route for severe crowding or protrusion.

lead: Extraction-free orthodontics, also called non-extraction orthodontics, is an approach in which crowding and bite problems are corrected without removing permanent teeth, most commonly first premolars. Space for alignment is created by other means such as arch expansion, distalizing molars, or slightly narrowing the teeth.[1]

People interested in facial aesthetics use it as a way to protect forward support of the lips and lower face. The reasoning is that extraction spaces, when closed, can retract the front teeth and flatten the lip profile, whereas keeping all teeth lets the arches keep or gain width. Orthodontists describe the decision as individual: severe protrusion of both jaws, for example, is frequently planned with extractions or surgery to bring the lips back.[2]

Research is mostly retrospective cephalometric studies and case reports rather than randomized trials. A retrospective cephalometric study of 112 patients with Class I crowding found that adolescents' lips moved forward and down during non-extraction treatment, while adults showed less change and thinner lips.[3]

chain: Keeps all teeth and widens or distalizes the arches
Front teeth and lips are not retracted by extraction-space closure
Fuller, more forward lip and lower-face support
angle.text: Non-extraction plans are chosen when people want alignment while preserving or adding lip and lower-face projection. The outcome depends on how crowded the teeth are and how the jaws relate, which the treating orthodontist measures.

paras: Orthodontic plans for crowding can be grouped into extraction and non-extraction approaches. Extraction plans, usually with removal of four premolars, create room for alignment and for retracting protruding front teeth. Non-extraction plans keep every tooth and gain space by expanding the arch width, proclining the incisors, distalizing molars or reducing enamel between teeth.[1]

Case reports describe the toolkit: a 10-year follow-up of twin sisters treated for crowding and midline deviation used a straight-wire system with arch expansion over 13 months,[4] and a 2025 case report treated severe crowding and open bite in a skeletal Class III patient by distalizing both arches with clear aligners and miniscrews.[5]

The debate dates to the early twentieth century. Edward Angle, often called the father of modern orthodontics, opposed extraction and held that perfect occlusion would produce good facial aesthetics. Charles Tweed, a former student, helped reintroduce extractions in the 1940s and 1950s to improve facial appearance and stability of results.[6] The modern discussion therefore centers on which patients benefit from which approach.

In the cephalometric study of 40 adults and 72 adolescents with Class I crowding, adolescent lips moved anteriorly and inferiorly during non-extraction treatment, while adult lips showed less inferior movement, little or no forward movement and a decrease in thickness. Males showed greater changes than females in some measures.[3]

For bimaxillary protrusion, a 2023 review proposes a severity-based classification to guide whether the case is treated with orthodontics alone or combined with segmental orthognathic surgery, noting that this is a clinical dilemma.[2]

Evidence consists mainly of retrospective cohort studies, cephalometric analyses and case reports. A retrospective study of 83 patients compared post-treatment stability of impacted-wisdom-tooth extraction with non-extraction orthodontics across age groups.[7] A 2025 retrospective cohort examined predictors of open gingival embrasures after non-extraction fixed treatment.[8] A 1998 analysis used matched samples of earlier patients to compare extraction and non-extraction Class II treatments for efficiency, stability and esthetics.[9] No large randomized trials directly comparing facial attractiveness after extraction and non-extraction plans are cited here.

Orthodontic reviews note that in cases of marked protrusion or severe crowding, non-extraction approaches may leave the incisors more forward or the arches limited by bone, and extractions or jaw surgery are used.[2] Open gingival embrasures (black triangles) have been studied as a possible result of non-extraction treatment.[8]

The topic is discussed alongside jaw and midface development, with some community members preferring expansion-based plans in the hope of keeping facial support. Orthodontists generally frame the choice around individual diagnosis.

timeline.event: Tweed reintroduces extraction partly to improve facial aesthetics.[6]
Retrospective comparison of extraction and non-extraction Class II treatments published.[9]
Cephalometric study of lip changes after non-extraction treatment.[3]
Review proposes classification for bimaxillary protrusion management.[2]
